html:
Mithridates VI was king of Pontus, on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia, from about 120 to 63 BCE, and the most stubborn enemy of the Roman Republic in the east. Greek in culture and Persian in descent, he was said to speak the languages of all the peoples he ruled and to have made himself immune to poison by taking small doses.

He built a Black Sea empire. He took Colchis and, around 108 BCE, the Bosporan Kingdom in the Crimea, whose grain fed his armies. Then he pressed on the small kingdoms of Anatolia that Rome protected.

He fought Rome in three Mithridatic Wars:

  • 89 to 85 BCE: he overran Roman Asia and in 88 BCE ordered the killing of the Romans and Italians living there, tens of thousands of people. Athens joined him. The fight over who would command against him set Sulla against Marius and began Rome's civil wars. Sulla took Athens and forced a peace.
  • 83 to 81 BCE: a short war with a Roman governor.
  • 73 to 63 BCE: he allied with the rebel Sertorius in Spain. Lucullus drove him out of Pontus, and from 66 BCE Pompey finished the job.

He fled to his Bosporan lands and planned to invade Italy from the north. When his son Pharnaces turned against him, he died at Panticapaeum in 63 BCE. The story goes that he tried to poison himself, the poison failed, and he had a guard kill him.
